    AI Overview
    A fillip (pronounced /ˈfɪl.ɪp/) is
    a stimulus, boost, or unexpected boost that encourages improvement or excitement. It also refers to a sharp, small tap made by snapping a finger against a thumb. Originating in the 15th century as a word for this finger-snap, it evolved to mean any small incentive. 
    Usage Examples 
    • "The tax reduction provided a much-needed fillip to the struggling housing market".
    • "The surprise announcement gave her campaign a significant fillip".
    • "The chef added a final fillip of parsley to the dish". 
    Synonyms
     
    • Stimulus, boost, encouragement, incentive, impetus, fillip, stimulus, stimulant.
    • Embellishment, addition, extra, twist, sparkle. 
    Antonyms 
    • Block, check, discouragement, hindrance, deterrent.

    Definitions from Oxford Languages · Learn more
    fil·lip
    /ˈfiləp/
    Learn to pronounce
    noun
    noun: fillip; plural noun: fillips
    1. 1.
      something which acts as a stimulus or boost to an activity.
      "the halving of the automobile tax would provide a fillip to sales"
      h
      Similar:
      stimulus
      stimulation
      stimulant
      boost
      encouragement
      incitement
      incentive
      impetus
      inducement
      motivation
      tonic
      uplift
      lift
      reviver
      spur
      goad
      prod
      push
      prompt
      aid
      help
      shot in the arm
      pick-me-up
      h
      Opposite:
      curb
    2. 2.
      archaic
      a movement made by bending the last joint of the finger against the thumb and suddenly releasing it; a flick of the finger.
      "the Prince, by a fillip, made some of the wine fly in Oglethorpe's face"
      • a slight smart stroke or tap.
        "she began to give him dainty fillips on the nose with a soft forepaw"
    verb
    archaic
    verb: fillip; 3rd person present: fillips; past tense: filliped; past participle: filliped; gerund or present participle: filliping
    1. propel (a small object) with a flick of the finger.
      "our aforesaid merchant filliped a nut sharply against his bullying giant"
      • strike (someone or something) slightly and smartly.
        "he filliped him over the nose"
      • stimulate or urge (someone or something).
        "pour, that the draught may fillip my remembrance"
    Origin
    late Middle English (in the sense ‘make a fillip with the fingers’): symbolic; compare with flick, flip1.
    Use over time for: fillip

    AI Overview
    A fillip is a noun referring to
    a stimulus, boost, or something that adds excitement (e.g., "the win gave the team a fillip"). It also means a quick, sharp tap made by snapping a finger against a thumb. Synonyms include boost, stimulus, encouragement, incentive, and flick. 
    Usage Examples: 
    • As a Stimulus: "The extra funding was a much-needed fillip for the arts program".
    • As an Addition/Enhancement: "A dash of lemon provided the perfect fillip to the dish".
    • As a Motion (Verb/Noun): "He sent the paper ball flying with a fillip of his finger". 
    Key Synonyms: 
    • Stimulus/Boost: Catalyst, incentive, encouragement, shot in the arm.
    • Action: Flick, tap, snap.

      AI Overview
      The word fillip is pronounced FIL-up (/ˈfɪlɪp/ or /ˈfɪləp/). It is pronounced exactly like the male name "Philip" or "Phillip," with the stress on the first syllable, a short "i" sound, and a light "p" at the end. 
      Key Pronunciation Details: 
      • IPA: /ˈfɪlɪp/
      • Phonetic: FILL-ip
      • Rhymes with: Philip, Phillip, fill-up
      • Syllables: fil-lip (two syllables)
      Fillip refers to a movement of the finger/thumb or something that acts as a stimulus or boost.

        AI Overview
        The word fillip operates as both a noun and a verb. As a noun, it means a stimulus, encouragement, or a smart tap made by flicking a finger. As a verb, it means to stimulate, excite, or to strike something using that specific finger-and-thumb action. 
        Here are the different parts of speech for fillip:
        • Noun:
          • Something that adds stimulation, encouragement, or excitement (e.g., "The news gave her a much-needed fillip"). 
          • A blow or tap made by snapping a finger against the thumb. 
        • Verb (transitive and intransitive):
          • To act as a stimulus; to encourage (e.g., "The tax cut filliped the economy"). 
          • To strike or project something sharply with a snap of the finger. 
        Synonyms include stimulus, boost, encouragement, incentive, and flick.

          Literary History. What is the history of the word fillip in literature?
          About this result

          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          "Fillip," emerging in the 15th-16th centuries from Middle English filippen (likely onomatopoeic for a finger snap), originally meant a sharp, flicking blow. It evolved from describing physical, often trivial, strikes in early literature to a figurative 18th-century meaning of a "stimulus" or "boost," often used to describe encouragement. 
          Key Historical Shifts in Literature:
          • 15th–16th Century (Physical Action):
            The word was used to describe the motion of bending a finger against the thumb and releasing it sharply, often a petty or mocking gesture. 
          • 16th–17th Century (Triviality):
            Used to represent something small or of no value, as seen in Lord Byron's usage, "the rest's not worth a fillip". 
          • 18th Century–Present (Stimulus):
            By the 18th and 19th centuries, it shifted to describe a boost, encouragement, or stimulus that adds vigor to an activity. 
          • Etymological Note:
            "Fillip" predates "flip" and "flick". It is often used in literature and formal contexts (e.g., The Economist) to describe a much-needed stimulant to the economy or spirits. 
          Literary Usage Examples:
          • Figurative Stimulus: "A drop in interest rates gave a welcome fillip to the housing market". 
          • Physical Act: "The prince, by a fillip, made some of the wine fly in Oglethorpe's face".
